newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Grammy Winner Brecker owes it all to Philadelphia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Grammy Winner Brecker owes it all to Philadelphia.

text.p: Michael Brecker, who picked up his second Grammy award in a row last month for instrumental jazz solo, is famed for an edgy and blue saxophone sound that he says he owes to Philadelphia.

Trace the personal histories of jazz musicians and often you wind up in a city -- New Orleans, Detroit, New York, Philadelphia, Kansas City, Pittsburgh -- each with its own rich history and distinctivre sound.

Clusters of musicians often come out of the same family, high school or era; they develop their sound, their language, in living rooms, clubs, garages or churches and years later, after they have left home and won over audiences worldwide, the roots are still recognisable.

In the late 1970s, the Brecker Brothers band -- Randy Brecker plays trumpet -- put the two on the map with an electric jazz-funk sound. Michael Brecker also played with a range of rock and pop stars like Joni Mitchell and Paul Simon.
For the past few years, both brothers have focused on mainstream jazz. In this setting, Michael, 47, has clearly emerged as a major voice on the tenor saxophone, something the Grammys recognised.

"I've never felt complete playing just electric or acoustic," Brecker told Reuters. "I always did both but I'm going through a phase where I like acoustic more ... and it always takes me a long time to learn things."
A MUSICAL FEEDING FRENZY

Philadelphia has been home to such luminaries as saxophonist John Coltrane, trumpeters Dizzy Gillespie and Clifford Brown, organist Jimmy Smith, pianist McCoy Tyner and the Heath brothers (bassist Percy, saxophonist Jimmy and drummer Albert "Tootie"), to name a few.
Brecker concedes he has been influenced by many of the Philadelphia horn players and by others like Wayne Shorter, who grew up in Newark, New Jersey, and Joe Henderson, who hails from Ohio.
When he recorded with Tyner in 1995 on the Grammy-winning recording Infinity, the two musicians hit a special groove. Asked about it, the pianist said, "Well, you know, we're both from Philadelphia."
Brecker, who left the city after high school, likes to return for concerts. Call it the home court advantage.

He recently ended a tour promoting his recent recording "Tales of the Hudson" (Impulse!) at the Theatre for the Living Arts here, and for two hours audience and musician engaged in what might be called a musical feeding frenzy.

When Brecker and his band -- bassist Dave Holland, drummer Jack DeJohnette, guitarist Pat Metheny and pianist Joey Calderazzo -- walked on stage they got a resounding welcome. The band returned the greeting with a ferocious Brecker tune, "Slings and Arrows," and the excitement never let up.
"It's always a treat to play in Philly," Brecker said a few days later. "The audiences there are great and my only regret is that I don't get to play there that often."
PASSIONATE BUT NOT PRETTY

The CD provides an example of what was at work that night, but it is often forgotten in the digital age that a recording can never capture all the vicissitudes of what occurs when a band is performing live, taking the music to fresh ground.
When he is playing, Brecker is passionate but not pretty and tends towards the gritty, frenetic edge of sounds. There is an ample taste of the blues and his music is infused with dark swing.

He is comfortable in a fast-paced environment -- the bebop-influenced "Cabin Fever" won his 1996 Grammy -- and on ballads like "Introduction to Naked Soul" he sounds more like a tortured angsty lover than a svelte Romeo.

With these emotional ingredients, he picked a stellar band for his recording and tour. Drummer DeJohnette feeds the intensity and the ideas measure-by-measure, while pianist Calderazzo adds his own off-centre rhythmic ideas. Metheny, a longtime collaborator, is the melodic one, always finding a tune within the tune. Holland grounds the swing.
All of that came to bear at the Philadelphia concert. When it was done, Brecker thanked his home town crowd and the band. "These are the best musicians I've ever played with," he said.
